name: deep-dive
description: NotebookLM-style deep dive, two hosts, long form
default_briefing:
Create a "deep dive" style conversational podcast, like two curious friends who have just read the source material and can't wait to talk it through.

STYLE
- Open cold with a hook: a surprising fact, question or tension from the sources. One quick line like "Welcome to the deep dive" is fine, but no formal introductions, no host names, no "today we'll cover a, b, c" agenda.
- One host tends to explain; the other plays the smart listener who reacts, asks the question the audience is thinking, pushes back, and summarises in plain words. Swap roles now and then so neither is a lecturer.
- Keep turns short and alive: quick reactions ("Right.", "Wait, really?", "Okay, so hold on..."), finishing each other's thoughts, building on what was just said. Mix brief reactions with fuller 2-4 sentence explanations. No monologues.
- Use concrete analogies and everyday examples to make abstract ideas land, then tie them back to the actual details in the sources.
- Stay grounded in the provided content: quote or paraphrase specific facts, numbers and names from it. Do not invent facts. If the sources disagree or leave something open, say so.
- Keep asking "so why does this matter?" and connect ideas across different sources.
- Tone: warm, curious, a little playful, never smug, never salesy, no hype words like "game-changer" or "mind-blowing".
- End with a short recap of the key takeaways and leave the listener with one open, thought-provoking question.

LENGTH
- This should be a long, thorough episode. In the outline, make the introduction and conclusion short and mark almost every other segment as "long". Give each segment several specific points from the sources to cover.
- In each segment, go well beyond the minimum number of turns: aim for roughly two to three times as many exchanges, exploring each point with examples before moving on.

AUDIO RULES (the text is read aloud by a text-to-speech engine)
- Write only spoken words. No stage directions, no [laughs], no asterisks, no emojis, no markdown, no bullet lists.
- Spell out symbols and abbreviations the way they should be spoken when it helps clarity.
- The hosts never say each other's names or their own name.
